how-to-price-carpet-cleaning.html.text:
CARPET CLEANING PRICING

How to price carpet cleaning without giving the drive away.

The search phrase is usually “carpet cleaning cost per room.” Almost every result is a lead form or a $99 three-bedroom special. This page is the method behind a number you can stand on, and it pairs with a free browser calculator that does the arithmetic locally.

The customer thinks in rooms. The clock does not.

A vacant 200 sq ft bedroom extracts faster than the same room after a dog has lived on it. Stairs are not a room. A sofa is not “included.” Forty minutes of windshield time is two wages if you brought a helper, and it is unpaid if you priced only the carpet. Quote three bedrooms as a package and you have hidden the lines that decide whether the stop prints money.

Build extraction first

Measure each room. Divide square feet by the rate your truck actually hits on that soil — vacant/light, normal household, or heavy / restoration. Those starting figures in the calculator are ballpark, not an IICRC standard. Time your own stops and replace them. The rooms that look the same on a floor plan are not the same job once soil is on the clock.

Then price the work a special cannot see

Flights of stairs, an extra extraction pass on pet-urine rooms plus the chemistry those rooms consume, each upholstery piece in minutes, furniture moving, and the round-trip drive. Payroll burden — employer tax, workers’ compensation, liability — belongs on the wage. A technician at $20 an hour is not a $20 hour.

Walk-away is cost, not the special

Overhead as a share of direct cost, then a target margin as a share of price, is how the customer number is built. A posted minimum (“$149 to roll the truck”) is a floor on that number. It is not a substitute for knowing cost. If a three-bedroom special is $129 and loaded labor plus chemistry plus the drive is $180, the special is a donation. Hold the walk-away and let the customer decide whether the house is worth it.

What this is not

Not a quote on your behalf, not an industry rate card, not legal or business advice. Rates vary by fibre, machine, region, and how long the soil has sat. Verify every figure against your own tickets before you send a price.

Open the carpet cleaning bid calculator — it stays in your browser.

Common questions

How do carpet cleaners charge?

Many advertise a per-room or three-bedroom special. The work is extraction time (square feet divided by a soil-specific rate), plus stairs, extra passes for pet urine, upholstery, furniture moving, and the drive. A room price that ignores those lines underprices a lived-in house.

How much should I charge for carpet cleaning per room?

There is no single number. Price per room is the bid divided by the rooms after labor, chemistry, overhead, and the drive are known, not a starting rate. Two 200 sq ft bedrooms are not the same job if one has pet urine and the other is vacant.

Why do three-bedroom specials lose money?

A posted special assumes light soil, no stairs, no pets, no sofa, and a short drive. Stairs, a second extraction pass, upholstery, furniture moving, or a 40-minute deadhead can put loaded labor above the special before anyone is paid.

No warranty. This page is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice. You are responsible for reviewing every number before relying on it.

Bid the stop, not the room special.

Price a carpet cleaning job the way the clock actually works: each room divided by the extraction rate that soil really takes, then stairs, pet-urine extra passes, the sofa, furniture moving, and the drive. You get the quote, what it works out to per room and per labor hour including windshield time, and the number below which a $129 three-bedroom special loses money.

One row per room. Production rate is carpet square feet one technician extracts per hour — pick a soil level to start from a common figure, then replace it with a rate timed from your own stops. Check pet treatment when that room needs an extra extraction pass.

Where the hours go

    Transparent arithmetic from your own inputs. The starting extraction rates are common ballpark figures, not an industry standard, a benchmark, or a guarantee — time your own stops and replace them.

    Hand the customer a proposal

    The price above is for you. This is the page you print or save as a PDF and give to the customer — your details, their details, the scope, the deposit split, and a line for them to sign. Your business details are saved on this device so you only type them once; the customer’s details are never saved.

    Everything on the printed page is text you typed or a number this calculator worked out. It contains no warranty, lien, or cancellation wording — those depend on your jurisdiction and your contract, and this tool is not the place to invent them.

    Common questions

    What does this quote actually add up?

    The price adds up extraction hours per room from the square footage and production rate you enter, an extra extraction pass on any room marked pet treatment, stairs by flight, upholstery piece by piece, furniture-moving minutes, and the round-trip drive — plus chemistry per square foot and per pet room, other job costs, overhead, and your target margin, then compares that to your posted minimum charge and quotes whichever is higher.

    What is the “hours that are not extraction” number, and why does it matter?

    It is every hour on the ticket that is not carpet extraction — stairs, pet extra passes, upholstery, furniture moving, and the drive. A posted per-room special is built on light-soil, vacant-room extraction time; stairs, a sofa, a pet room, and the windshield time to get there are exactly the hours that special leaves off, which is why a “3 bedroom special” that looked full on the schedule can still lose money once they are added back in.

    Why does a pet-treatment room cost more than the same square footage without it?

    A pet-treated room gets an extra extraction pass — by default a full second pass at the same production rate — on top of the normal extraction hours for that room’s square footage, plus its own line of pet chemistry cost. Two rooms of identical size price differently once one of them is marked for pet treatment.

    Is my data uploaded anywhere?

    No account and no network requests — the calculator runs entirely in your browser, and nothing about the job is sent anywhere. A share link encodes only the rooms, upholstery, and rates you choose into the address bar and is never sent to us; only your business details for the printed proposal are kept in this browser’s local storage so you do not retype them, and the customer’s details are never saved.

    What does “minimum applied” mean?

    It shows whether your posted minimum charge ended up higher than the price the job’s own hours and costs would have produced. On a small stop — one light room and a short drive — the minimum is usually what you actually quote; on a house with stairs, pets, and upholstery, the job price passes the minimum on its own.

    Does this check drying time, mold risk, or whether a carpet is worth cleaning?

    No. Production rates and chemistry costs are ballpark shop figures you can edit, not a moisture-control assessment, a mold-risk determination, or a guarantee that a given stain, pet odor, or worn carpet will come clean. Whether a carpet is salvageable, how long it needs to dry, and what soil level a specific room really is are still a judgment call from the walkthrough — this tool prices the job you describe, it does not inspect it.

vs-a-flat-per-room-special.html.text:
← Carpet Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. a flat per-room special

“3 bedrooms, $129, done” is not a price for a carpet-cleaning stop — it is a price for one soil level and one scope, quietly applied to every house that calls in.

What a flat per-room special is

A flat per-room special is the fastest way to quote a carpet-cleaning stop over the phone: name a room count, read back a price. Customers shop it because it is easy to compare between competitors' postcards, and it is the number a customer holding a flyer will ask you to match.

The number behind it was set for one kind of stop — usually a vacant or light-soil house, no pet-treated rooms, no stairs, nothing to move, and a short drive — and then reused for every house afterward, whether or not the next one has pets, stairs, furniture on the carpet, or sits forty minutes round trip away.

What this calculator is

This page keeps no account and sends nothing to a server. You enter each room's square footage and soil-specific extraction rate, which rooms need a pet-treatment extra pass, stairs, upholstery, furniture-moving minutes, and the round-trip drive, plus your own wage, payroll burden, chemical cost, overhead, and target margin. It prices the extraction hours by soil and room, adds pet passes, stairs, upholstery, furniture moving, and drive time as their own buckets, and returns the price, the price per room, and the effective hourly rate — for this stop, not a flat number for every house.

What a flat per-room special doesWhat this calculator does instead
Charges the same fee whether the house is vacant and light-soil or normal household soil that extracts at a slower square-foot-per-hour rate. Prices extraction hours from a soil-specific rate per room — light, normal, or heavy — so a more heavily soiled house costs more without anyone eyeballing a surcharge.
Has no line for pet urine at all — a house with two pet-treated rooms gets the same quote as one with none. Prices pet-treated rooms with their own extra extraction pass and their own chemistry cost, as a first-class input rather than a judgment call at the door.
Quotes the same number for a one-story ranch and a two-story house with flights of stairs, with no separate line for the stairs. Prices stairs by the flight, at minutes you set, so a two-story stop is never quoted at the ranch's price.
Has no line for moving furniture off the carpet before it can be cleaned, and none for the drive to get there. Prices furniture-moving minutes and round-trip drive time as their own buckets, so a stop with both is never quoted as if the crew showed up empty-handed and already on site.
Gives the technician a number to quote, not a number to check a quote against. Reports the price per room, the effective hourly rate, and the walk-away price, so a shopped special can be scored against real cost before you commit to it.

Two 5-room, 820 sq ft stops, one flat price

Using this calculator's own shipped starting example:

A 5-room, 820 sq ft house — living room, three bedrooms, and a hall — that is vacant, light-soil, with no stairs, nothing to move, and a short drive, prices at $221.64 on a stop that takes 3.1 hours.

Take the identical 5 rooms and 820 square feet and make it a lived-in house instead — normal household soil, two pet-treated rooms each needing an extra extraction pass, two flights of stairs, 25 minutes of furniture moving, and a 40-minute round-trip drive — and the stop takes 6.2 hours, double the easy house's time on the identical room count. It costs $264.43 to run before a dollar of profit, and this calculator prices it at $406.81. Quoting the harder stop at the easier stop's rounded flat special of $220 prices it $44.43 below its own break-even cost — before counting the $186.81 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 35% target margin. Same room count, same flat price, one stop that pays and one that loses money the moment the pets, the stairs, and the drive show up.

Common questions

Why does a flat per-room special get a carpet-cleaning stop wrong?

Because the cost driver is the soil, the add-ons, and the drive, not the room count. A 5-room, 820 sq ft house that is vacant, light-soil, has no stairs, nothing to move, and is five minutes away needs about 3.1 hours of work. The identical 5-room, 820 sq ft house with normal household soil, two pet-treated rooms needing an extra extraction pass, two flights of stairs, 25 minutes of furniture moving, and a 40-minute round-trip drive needs about 6.2 hours -- double the time, on the identical room count. A flat per-room special charges both the same because it was priced on rooms, not on soil, add-ons, or the drive.

What does a flat per-room special usually leave out entirely?

Pet urine's extra extraction pass, stairs, furniture moving, and the drive. A flat price has no line for a pet-treated room needing a second pass through the same square footage, no line for a flight of stairs at a fixed number of minutes each, no line for moving furniture off a carpet before it can be cleaned, and no separate line for the drive at all -- it is usually priced as if the crew is already on site. On this calculator's own shipped starting example, that hidden work -- pet passes, stairs, furniture, and the drive together -- is 52.7% of the total time on the job, more than half the stop, on top of the extraction itself.

How big is the pricing gap in practice?

On this calculator's own shipped starting example: a 5-room, 820 sq ft house that is vacant, light-soil, with no stairs, nothing to move, and a short drive prices at $221.64, on a job that takes 3.1 hours. The identical 5-room, 820 sq ft house with two pet-treated rooms, two flights of stairs, 25 minutes of furniture moving, and a 40-minute round-trip drive takes 6.2 hours and costs $264.43 to run before a dollar of profit -- this calculator prices that stop at $406.81. Quoting the harder stop at the easier stop's rounded flat price of $220 prices it $44.43 below its own break-even cost, before counting the $186.81 it falls short of this calculator's own price at a 35% target margin. Same room count, same flat price, one stop that pays and one that loses money the moment the pets, the stairs, and the drive show up.

Is a flat per-room special ever the right way to quote?

For a narrow band of similar stops -- a vacant or light-soil house, no pet rooms, no stairs, nothing to move, and a short drive -- a flat per-room number can land close, because that is probably the stop the price was set on. The risk is quoting a normal-to-heavy-soil house, a stop with pet-treated rooms or several flights of stairs, or one with a long drive the same way sight unseen, because the price does not know the soil, the add-ons, or the drive until someone is standing in the house, and by then the flat number has often already been quoted.

Does this calculator know my local labor rates or chemical costs?

No. It has no data on your local labor market or your chemical supplier's pricing. It takes each room's square footage and soil-specific extraction rate, pet treatment, stairs, upholstery, furniture moving, and the drive, and your own wage, payroll burden, chemical cost, other job cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into a price for this stop -- the arithmetic a flat per-room special skips, not a market survey.

Open the Carpet Cleaning Bid Calculator to price your own stop, or read the pricing walkthrough.

No warranty. This free tool is not legal, tax, financial, or business advice, and it does not tell you what to charge. It is not a soil assessment, a specification, or a finding that any stop is ready to clean. Verify every figure against your own payroll, chemical costs, and a qualified professional before relying on it or submitting a bid. To the maximum extent permitted by law, the authors accept no liability for loss or damage from its use.

Nothing leaves your browser. Every number stays on this device, and this page makes no live comparison against any competing service — it is a static page describing the calculator's own worked example.

← Carpet Cleaning Bid Calculator

This calculator vs. ServiceMonster

Two different shapes: ServiceMonster is account-based field-service management software for running a carpet-cleaning company's whole operation. This page is a free, private worksheet for one question — what should this one stop cost, given its rooms, soil level, and add-ons, before you quote it.

What each tool is for

ServiceMonster is field-service management software with roots going back to 2002 as software built specifically for carpet cleaners, headquartered in Bellingham, Washington. It markets today to carpet cleaning, window cleaning, pressure washing, and related cleaning trades. It combines customer and account management, job scheduling and technician routing, estimates and invoicing, and automated marketing campaigns into one subscription system, with a mobile app for crews in the field. ServiceMonster's own marketing says it is trusted by thousands of service pros, and industry coverage reports it was acquired in 2023 by Teamfront. It is sold as an ongoing subscription account. ServiceMonster's own pricing page is not reachable from this session to confirm today's exact plan names or dollar figures, so no price for it is invented here: only its well-documented identity and category — cleaning-industry field-service management software, sold as a subscription account — are stated, and no dollar amount for ServiceMonster appears on this page.

This calculator does none of what ServiceMonster does. It does not manage customer accounts, route technicians across a schedule, or run marketing campaigns, and it stores no customer or job record on a server. It takes one stop's rooms, each with its own square footage and a soil-specific extraction rate (vacant/light, normal household, heavy/restoration), with stairs as flights, a second extraction pass for pet-urine rooms, upholstery pieces timed in minutes, furniture moving, and round-trip drive time, plus loaded wage, chemistry cost, overhead, and target margin, and turns that into the per-stop price, the price per room and per square foot, the effective hourly rate including the drive, the on-site rate without it, and the walk-away price below which the stop loses money — plus, if you already have a price on the table, a check of whether it clears that walk-away floor, and a copyable plain-text bid summary. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and uploads nothing you type.

This page's own figures are a pricing model, not a scheduled job, an invoice, or a signed proposal.

This tool needs no account and no sign-in: it is a static page, the arithmetic runs in your browser, and once it has loaded it keeps working with the connection off.

Should I use this calculator or ServiceMonster?

They do different jobs, and a carpet-cleaning operator of any size will likely end up touching both eventually.
